vectors.name: formats-toml/basic/array-of-tables-becomes-repeated-edges
vectors.comment: [[x]] is TOML's idiomatic repeated record and lands on the repeated-label shape with no adjustment needed -- of the four non-native formats, TOML's own idiom already matches the Document model.

vectors.name: formats-toml/temporals/native-date-time-and-datetime-all-resolve-with-no-schema
vectors.comment: TOML is the one format with native literals for all three temporal kinds -- and, unlike YAML, a bare time-of-day resolves correctly to `time` rather than a sexagesimal integer. Confirmed live.

vectors.name: formats-toml/nulls/null-leaf-cannot-be-written
vectors.comment: TOML has no null, and there is no substitute value to fall back to -- dropping the edge would erase its existence, not just its value, silently. The write fails unconditionally, not only under strict (2026-08-24: this vector previously expected ok:true with format.null-unrepresentable and a still-succeeding write; that was found to be the same class of problem as the XML label-sanitization collision bug -- silent, unrecoverable data loss with no way to detect it happened).

vectors.name: formats-toml/nulls/null-leaf-cannot-be-written-strict-is-the-same
vectors.comment: Companion to formats-toml/nulls/null-leaf-cannot-be-written, differing only in strict:true -- confirms the failure is unconditional, not a strict-mode-only behavior. Both vectors MUST produce the identical result.

vectors.name: formats-toml/encoding/leading-bom-is-stripped
vectors.comment: D-15, the TOML half. A BOM carries no data -- it is meaningless for UTF-8, which has no byte-order ambiguity to mark -- so treating it as content on some surfaces and not others is how two implementations build different Documents from one file. Paired with the JSON and OSD vectors because those were the three readers that rejected a BOM before D-15.

vectors.name: formats-toml/encoding/doubled-leading-bom-is-rejected
vectors.comment: D-21: D-15 consumes exactly one leading U+FEFF and stops, and a reader MUST then reject a second mark still standing at offset zero of what remains. That is a rule Omnist imposes, not one read off each format -- the formats disagree, and this vector's own note below says what this one would do unaided. The position is 1:1 because it is computed on the text remaining after the strip, not on the original input. TOML is the third surface where the rule costs nothing, for the opposite reason to OML and OSD: TOML v1.0.0's grammar gives U+FEFF no position anywhere, leading or otherwise, so rejecting the second mark is TOML's ordinary behavior and D-15's strip of the first is the deliberate Omnist addition. Measured: the reference rejects the input but emits parse.syntax with no path at all (DIV-4).

vectors.name: formats-toml/encoding/invalid-utf8-byte-above-the-range-is-rejected
vectors.comment: D-14 on TOML, with the out-of-range class: `f5` starts a four-byte sequence for a code point at or above U+140000, and Unicode stops at U+10FFFF, so no continuation bytes can rescue it -- `f5 80 80 80` is malformed however it is read. TOML's own specification already requires a valid UTF-8 document, so unlike D-15's BOM strip this rule asks nothing of a TOML reader that TOML did not already ask; what D-14 adds is the code and the path. Measured against the Python reference (v0.9.5) 2026-09-21: its readers take `str`, so these bytes cannot be handed to one at all, and its CLI decodes both file and stdin input strictly -- `open(path, encoding="utf-8")` and a utf-8/strict `sys.stdin` -- so it fails with an uncaught UnicodeDecodeError and no diagnostic rather than reporting this code. No silent repair, but not conformant either; recorded as DIV-6. The other four ports were not measured for this vector.

vectors.name: formats-toml/encoding/valid-multi-byte-characters-are-accepted
vectors.comment: The TOML control: the same three characters as the other surfaces' controls, given as bytes. Measured against the Python reference (v0.9.5) 2026-09-21: accepted, this exact Document.
